title: "seen, Sita"
hook: a hair jewel, a story only Rama would know, and a month on the clock: the beautiful book comes to rest

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman put seen first, so Rama's fear was answered before the story began, and your line, he arranges his words around Rama's fear. Did you lead with the word someone needed? Today, what Hanuman carried back in his hand, and the last page of the Sundara Kanda. Day six hundred thirty-three.

Hanuman has told the story. Now he opens his hand. In it is a jewel, a small ornament Sita wore in her hair. In the ashoka grove she untied it and gave it to him, so that Rama would believe every word. Rama takes it and holds it against his chest, and he weeps. Lakshmana stands beside him. To anyone else it's an ornament. To the two men looking at it, it's her. That's where the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, comes to rest.
screen: `HANUMAN OPENS HIS HAND.` → `A JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` → `RAMA WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Rama knows the jewel at once. In Valmiki he says it came to Sita from her father, King Janaka, at their wedding, and that seeing it is almost like seeing her. Then he asks Hanuman again and again: what did she say? Tell me her exact words. So Hanuman passes on everything. Sita had given him a second token besides the jewel, and it was a story. Long before, at Chitrakuta, a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, roused, sent a single blade of grass after it as a weapon. Nobody else was there. Only Rama would know. A memory used as a password. And she sent a message with a deadline. She would hold on for one more month, she said. After that she would not live. So the joy of seen arrives with a clock attached. Rama's grief and his resolve rise together. Why is this book called Sundara, beautiful? People give different answers, and nobody can say for certain which one Valmiki meant. But Hindu tradition treats the Sundara Kanda as a book of hope. It's recited on its own, start to finish, at home or in a temple, especially in hard times, because it's the stretch of the story where the lost is found and the long wait finally hears seen. And notice how it ends. Not on the leap, not on the burning city. It ends on a man holding a hair ornament and asking to hear her words one more time.
screen: `HER FATHER'S JEWEL.` · `A MEMORY AS A PASSWORD.` · `ONE MORE MONTH.` · `THE BOOK OF HOPE.` · then, large: `TELL ME HER WORDS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your hands rest open in your lap. Think of one small object that holds a person for you: a ring, a note, a cup, a photo, an old shirt. You don't need to fetch it. Just see it, and let the person come with it. Breathe in, and feel how much a small thing can carry. Breathe out, and let whatever comes up settle. The bell holds the time.
Seen, Sita. The news that closes the Sundara Kanda, carried home with a jewel from her hair, a story only Rama would know, and one month on the clock.
Your line: tell me her words again. Today, notice one small object that carries someone for you, and let it. Tomorrow the war book begins. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Hindu families and temples recite the Sundara Kanda on its own as a complete reading, often over several days and especially in difficult times, and it closes with Rama holding Sita's jewel.

fork.setup: you're Rama. Hanuman has just put Sita's jewel in your hand. what do you do?
options: call the army to march at once.
weep, and ask to hear her words again.
fork.reveal: he knows it at once, holds it to his chest and weeps, and asks Hanuman to tell him again exactly what she said.

original.note: Sanskrit cūḍāmaṇi: crest jewel, from cūḍā, the crown of the head, and maṇi, jewel.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita sent a jewel as proof she was alive.
what it means: she sent a jewel, a private memory and a one-month deadline: proof, password and plea.
what a scholar hears: the Sundara Kanda is recited on its own as a pārāyaṇa, a complete devotional reading, for hope in hard times.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 65–68 (the jewel given to Rama; Rama's grief; Sita's message retold)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 38 (the crow at Chitrakuta; the jewel; Sita's one month)

notes: The index word is "seen (with the opening quotation mark), kept exactly; see day 632's note.
Rama's account of the jewel's origin (from Janaka at the wedding; some versions add that it first came from Indra or from the waters): confirm.
Sita's one-month limit: confirm the sarga (Sundara 38 or 40 in the vulgate).
The crow episode is kept short; the crow's identity (Indra's son, named Jayanta in later tradition) is left out.
The reasons for the name Sundara are deliberately not listed; confirm that saying nobody can be certain is fair.
Pārāyaṇa of the Sundara Kanda: described as common, without a claim about how many families do it.
Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed the garbled 'jewel worth nothing special' line (a crest jewel is not worthless); removed 'many Hindus' and 'years before' (claims rule).
